schema.headline: Website & App Project Brief Checklist
schema.description: A practical website and app project brief: goals, users, workflows, integrations, budget, remote delivery and handover. By developer Sayan Mondal.
schema.articleBody:
Start with the business task
Describe the problem in ordinary language. A grocery shop may want customers to order without repeated phone calls. A service business may need customers to book and track a pickup. An internal team may need to stop entering the same information into several systems. State what should become easier and how you would recognize a useful result. You do not need to choose a framework first.

Identify the users and their main journey
List who will use the product: customers, staff, store managers or delivery partners, for example. Then write the essential steps each person needs to complete. Include the awkward cases, such as a failed payment, unavailable item, cancelled booking or interrupted connection. Those details often affect the work more than the number of screens.

Choose a useful first release
Separate what must work at launch from improvements that can follow. A responsive website may be enough for discovery and enquiries. A web app may fit an account-based workflow. A mobile app may be appropriate for device capabilities or frequent use. A developer should be able to explain the tradeoff using your users and requirements rather than treating every business as the same project.

List the systems the product must connect to
Note existing websites, APIs, spreadsheets, accounting tools, CRM, payment services and messaging channels. Identify who owns each account and whether documentation or test access is available. Mention any existing design or code. Do not paste passwords, customer records or private keys into a public enquiry; arrange a suitable access method after the scope is understood.

Make the estimate assumptions explicit
Share your preferred launch window, any fixed business deadline and a budget range with its currency if you have one. Explain what content, branding, designs and internal review capacity are already available. A useful proposal should distinguish included work, exclusions, third-party charges, revision expectations and maintenance. Price and timing need these assumptions; a universal app-development price would hide meaningful differences.

Agree how remote collaboration will work
Include your country, time zone, decision-maker and preferred review times. Discuss how questions, demos, approvals and change requests will be handled. I work from Kolkata, India and am available for remote projects worldwide. Communication overlap and project responsibilities should be agreed for the particular engagement, rather than assumed from the location of either party.

Plan ownership, deployment and handover
Before the build starts, agree repository and account access, ownership terms, hosting responsibilities, domain control and how credentials are shared. Define the acceptance checks, deployment process and handover material. If the product holds important data, discuss backups and recovery separately from release rollback. Clarify which post-launch fixes or support are included and which require a separate arrangement.

Use evidence when comparing a developer or agency
Ask to inspect relevant work and understand the supplier’s actual contribution. An attractive screenshot is useful, but also ask how the underlying workflow, integrations and release process were handled. The SayanTheCoder portfolio contains real supplied app, storefront, CRM, POS and deployment interfaces. Those examples help us discuss related requirements; they are not a promise that another business’s product can be reproduced unchanged.

schema.headline: Opslin: simpler VPS deployment and AI-assisted DevOps
schema.description: Sayan Mondal, founder of Opslin, explains deploying to your own Linux VPS, Git releases, monitoring, rollback and permissioned AI operations with MCP beta.
schema.articleBody:
Why I founded Opslin
I’m Sayan Mondal, founder of Opslin and Shotlin. I build products across interfaces, backend services and the infrastructure that runs them. Opslin grew from a practical problem: getting useful software online often takes far more operational work than the application itself suggests.
A working app still needs a runtime, a domain, HTTPS, environment variables, a database and a repeatable release process. After launch, someone must watch logs, investigate failures and know how to return to a working version. Opslin brings those related tasks into one deployment control plane for a VPS you control.

What problem does Opslin solve?
Manual server administration can scatter one release across a terminal, a hosting dashboard, separate monitoring tools and deployment scripts. When something fails, identifying the relevant logs and the last healthy release becomes another task. Opslin connects the application and its operational context so the next step is easier to find.
The aim is practical DevOps automation: repeat common deployment steps, keep application health visible and make recovery accessible. This can help developers, founders and small teams spend less time coordinating tools. It does not remove the need to understand application requirements, manage access or plan backups for important data.

From your Linux VPS to a running application
Start with a supported Linux VPS you own or rent. Use the setup command generated by the Opslin dashboard to connect its outbound agent. The agent connects from your server to the control plane; your application continues to run on your infrastructure.
Next, connect a GitHub repository or upload your application. Configure the runtime, application settings, secrets and domain for that workload. Opslin’s release workflow brings builds, deployments, health checks and rollback together, with domains and SSL alongside the application. Runtime targets include Node.js, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Java, Rust and static sites; check current compatibility for your framework and server.
An easier deployment flow still needs a valid configuration. Before routing real users to a release, check its logs, domain, HTTPS, database connection and health. Keep a recovery plan suited to the application rather than treating a successful build as proof that every feature is working.

Cloud operations after the first deploy
Deployment is the beginning of operating a product. Opslin’s dashboard connects fleet status, application details, deployment activity, domains, logs and metrics. Server monitoring covers CPU, memory, disk and network activity, helping you connect an application problem with the machine running it.
Database views bring supported PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and Redis instances into the same operational picture. Health checks, alerts and release rollback help teams investigate and respond when a change goes wrong. A release rollback and a database restore solve different problems: plan data recovery separately for stateful workloads.

AI-assisted deployment with Opslin MCP beta
Opslin MCP connects compatible AI assistants to supported deployment operations. Instead of copying logs between tools, you can ask an assistant to inspect the latest release, read logs, check health or perform an allowed deploy or rollback action. The connection is permissioned: the assistant’s available actions depend on the access you grant.
This is AI-assisted DevOps with a defined operating boundary. Review the requested action, target application and environment before an important change. An assistant can help interpret a failure or operate a supported workflow; it does not guarantee that a release is correct, secure or suitable for production.

Own the server and keep the workflow connected
Opslin’s bring-your-own-VPS approach separates infrastructure ownership from the deployment control plane. You choose the provider and server that fit your workload, while Opslin connects common operations in one interface. This suits teams that want a guided deployment experience on infrastructure they control.
My work as Opslin’s founder spans the Next.js dashboard, backend and outbound Go agent. It connects my software engineering and cloud development work with the daily DevOps needs of people shipping applications. Opslin is my independent product, built around a guided deployment experience and customer-controlled infrastructure.

What you can use today and what comes next
The official Opslin website currently presents the deployment platform and MCP as beta offerings. Beta access, supported actions and limits can change, so check the current product documentation before planning a rollout.
Launchpad is planned to help people discover suitable infrastructure. Marketplace is planned for deployment-ready software, templates, tools and experts. Both are marked coming soon. To explore what is available now, start with the official Opslin website and its current onboarding guidance.
